UN General Assembly resolutions are not formally a source of international law under Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute, because they are generally non-binding recommendations. They can still matter indirectly. They may be evidence of customary international law (opinio juris), as the ICJ reasoned in *Nicaragua* and *Nuclear Weapons*, and they can help interpret treaties or crystallise emerging norms. Some exceptions bind, such as internal budgetary or organisational decisions and resolutions that restate existing binding law (for example, the Declaration on Friendly Relations).
